articles.title: THX-02: a 4.5B open decision model that beats 27B models — and the API is free
articles.excerpt: Most of what AI does inside a real product is not writing essays. It is deciding. Which team owns this ticket. Is this message phishing. Does this applicant pass the policy. What is the next action. W…
articles.body: Most of what AI does inside a real product is not writing essays. It is deciding. Which team owns this ticket. Is this message phishing. Does this applicant pass the policy. What is the next action. Which of these 40 categories does this document belong to. Today teams pick between two bad options. A large chat model: slow, expensive per call, and it will happily invent a label that was never on your list. Or a narrow classifier: fast and cheap, but you retrain it for every new task, and it gives you a score you cannot explain to anyone. There is a third path. A model built for decisions only. You send it a state — text, JSON, or up to four images — plus typed questions, and it returns a probability for every option you supplied.
articles.author: FX-LgLL

articles.title: Server-Sent Events in Node.js: A Real-Time Dashboard That Survives Reconnects
articles.excerpt: Most real-time dashboard demos stop at the happy path: new EventSource('/events'), a chart, done. Then a laptop switches Wi-Fi networks, the stream drops for a second, and the chart quietly skips a fe…
articles.body: Most real-time dashboard demos stop at the happy path: new EventSource('/events'), a chart, done. Then a laptop switches Wi-Fi networks, the stream drops for a second, and the chart quietly skips a few dozen points. Nobody notices until the dashboard totals stop matching the database. Server-sent events (SSE) already include most of what you need to avoid that: event ids, automatic reconnection, and a Last-Event-ID header the browser sends when it reconnects. The browser side comes for free. The server side is up to you, and that is where the gaps usually are.

articles.title: Winback Email Works When It Knows Why They Left
articles.excerpt: The standard winback sequence is sorted by time: day 30, day 60, day 90, escalating discounts until somebody bites or unsubscribes. It treats every former subscriber as the same person — someone who w…
articles.body: The standard winback sequence is sorted by time: day 30, day 60, day 90, escalating discounts until somebody bites or unsubscribes. It treats every former subscriber as the same person — someone who weighed the product and found it wanting — and it fails most expensively on the group it never identifies: the subscribers who did not choose to leave at all. Their payment failed, the recovery sequence ended, and the account closed. Sending that group a 'we miss you, here is 20 percent off' email misdiagnoses them twice. They never rejected the product, and the fix they need is not a discount; it is a working payment path. A reason-sorted winback program splits the file before writing a word.

articles.title: I Turned My Laptop's Idle 6GB of VRAM Into Swap and It Stopped Crawling at 90% RAM
articles.excerpt: Two IDEs, Chrome with too many tabs, and Steam updating a game in the background. That's a normal afternoon on my Lenovo LOQ, and it's exactly when the laptop starts to feel like it's wading through m…
articles.body: Two IDEs, Chrome with too many tabs, and Steam updating a game in the background. That's a normal afternoon on my Lenovo LOQ, and it's exactly when the laptop starts to feel like it's wading through mud. The RAM meter sits at 90%. Clicking a tab takes a second. Switching back to the IDE takes three. Nothing crashes. It just gets slow, and then slower. The machine has 16 GB of RAM, one SODIMM, and an RTX 3050 with 6 GB of its own memory. That GPU memory was doing almost nothing. On this laptop the screen is driven by the Intel GPU, so unless I start a game, the NVIDIA card sits there holding a few hundred megabytes and waiting. So I built USM , which makes that idle VRAM the first place Linux swaps to. The code is on GitHub , MIT licensed, in beta.

It's great for newsrooms, content teams, social media managers and anyone building "what's hot" dashboards. Getting it into code is harder than it looks: The RSS feed is tiny. https://trends.google.com/trending/rss?geo=US is easy to parse, but it carries only around 10 trends, while the page itself lists hundreds. There's no official API for the Trending Now list. pytrends is archived and doesn't cover the current Trending Now page. If the top 10 is enough for you, use the RSS feed with feedparser and you're done.

articles.title: Theorem-Guided Decentralized Federated Learning & Cryptographic Runtime
articles.excerpt: Inspiration As decentralized networks scale toward millions of nodes, trusting the mathematical and cryptographic integrity of aggregation paths becomes non-negotiable. Sovereign-Mohawk-Proto (Mobile…
articles.body: Inspiration As decentralized networks scale toward millions of nodes, trusting the mathematical and cryptographic integrity of aggregation paths becomes non-negotiable. Sovereign-Mohawk-Proto (Mobile Offloading Heterogeneous Adaptive Weight for Knowledge) was built to bridge this gap—combining high-performance decentralized runtime layers with machine-checked Lean 4 formal verification artifacts. But writing proofs is only half the battle; validating them under adversarial real-world conditions requires rigorous, community-driven peer review. What It Does Sovereign-Mohawk-Proto is a 4-tier decentralized federated learning runtime featuring: Machine-Checked Formal Verification: Core cryptographic components and protocol assumptions backed by Lean 4 specifications.

articles.title: Earth has captured a new mini moon  — but it won't stick around for long
articles.excerpt: Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and QQ8 is sticking around for Christmas.
articles.body: Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and it is sticking around for Christmas. The space rock, designated 2026 QQ8, was first observed in August 2026 after entering orbit around Earth in April 2026. The discovery was reported by the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center on Thursday (Oct. 29). The stay of QQ8 is a temporary one. The mini-moon will remain in the thrall of Earth's gravity through December before breaking away in 2027. Scientists have recreated the orbital path of QQ8, finding that it takes 359 days, or about 0.98 of an Earth year, to orbit the sun . QQ8 closely approaches Earth around once every ten years, but this time the object came so close that Earth has been able to gravitationally seize it.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 5, 2002: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by Jupiter moon Almathea only to find it's a 'pile of icy rubble less dense than water'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 5, 2002, NASA's old Galileo spacecraft flew by a small moon called Amalthea and made a surprising find. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 5, 2002, NASA's old Galileo spacecraft was almost out of fuel. But the Jupiter mission still had some science to do. Galileo flew by a small moon called Amalthea. Amalthea is small, but it's interesting for scientists. The Jupiter moon Amalthea is the reddest object in our solar system. It also generates more heat than it gets from the sun. Scientists think Amalthea creates electrical currents as it orbits in Jupiter's huge magnetic field. Near this little moon, strong radiation from Jupiter is dangerous for spacecraft. The flyby caused some problems for Galileo. The spacecraft went into safe mode only 30 minutes after going past Amalthea. NASA said it was ready for problems, because Galileo was on its last legs, and the radiation near Amalthea was strong.

articles.title: You don't have to go to the moon to see Earth differently: Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover on what really matters
articles.excerpt: After a record-breaking journey around the moon, Artemis 2 astronaut Victor Glover explains why you don't need to travel into space to see Earth differently.
articles.body: TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Imagine traveling over 250 million miles from home, watching Earth disappear behind the moon and losing contact with the billions of people who call it home. What would you miss most? For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, the answer wasn't a particular place, a familiar view or even the comforts of home. It was something much more fundamental: human connection. Speaking during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival on Oct. 18 in Tenerife, Canary Islands, Glover reflected on the extraordinary experience of traveling around the moon and how being so far from Earth had given him a renewed appreciation for the people living on it. "The greatest reason to go to space, it isn't to be a swashbuckler hero," Glover said.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 probe bounces back from communications glitch in interstellar space
articles.excerpt: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is back in communication after the 49-year-old spacecraft briefly fell silent last month, during its interstellar-space mission.
articles.body: Voyager, 1, humanity's most distant spacecraft, is back in contact after briefly losing touch with Earth last month. The spacecraft stopped phoning home for about 48 hours between Oct. 18 and 20 due to a communications glitch that Voyager 1 resolved on its own, before engineers could send the long-running spacecraft a remote fix. "This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in an agency statement about the incident on Oct. 29.
